question.text: A 62-year-old man seeks evaluation at a local walk-in clinic for mid-low back pain of several weeks. He has tried different rehabilitation therapies and medications with no improvement. He was prescribed some pain medications and sent home last week, but the patient presents today with difficulty walking and worsening of his back pain. He was referred to the ER, where he was examined and found to have hypoesthesia from T12 to S4–S5, significant muscle weakness in both lower limbs, and reduced knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes. A hypotonic anal sphincter with conserved deep anal pressure was demonstrated on digital rectal examination, as well as a multinodular, asymmetric prostate. Imaging studies showed multiple sclerotic bone lesions along the spine. Subsequently, a prostate core biopsy was obtained which confirmed the diagnosis of prostate cancer. Which of the following characteristics would you expect in the specimen?

options.B: Well-formed glands with an increase in interglandular stroma

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's presentation strongly suggests metastatic prostate cancer to the spine. The key findings are the sclerotic bone lesions, hypoesthesia, muscle weakness, and reduced reflexes, all consistent with spinal cord compression. The prostate core biopsy confirming prostate cancer further supports this diagnosis. Given the metastatic nature of the cancer, the prostate specimen would likely show features consistent with the primary tumor. Small, closely-packed, well-formed glands are characteristic of prostate adenocarcinoma, the most common type of prostate cancer.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The prostate core biopsy confirming the diagnosis of prostate cancer.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (A) is a pre-cancerous condition, but the biopsy confirmed cancer. Well-formed glands with increased stroma (B) is a feature of prostate adenocarcinoma, but the description of the glands is more specific. Perineural invasion (C) is a common feature of prostate cancer, but it's not the most specific finding to expect in a biopsy. Fat invasion (D) is less common and would be a more advanced stage of metastasis. Small, closely-packed, well-formed glands (E) is the most characteristic finding in a biopsy of prostate adenocarcinoma, which is the most likely diagnosis given the clinical picture.

This aggressive disease pattern would lead to fat invasion in the prostate tissue, a characteristic feature of high-grade malignancies.

Perineural invasion (C) and fat invasion (D) are more characteristic of high-grade prostate cancer, which explains the clinical presentation and imaging findings.
